object.description: A scrap of papyrus the size of a postcard, dug out of the rubbish mounds of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt by Grenfell and Hunt in 1896-97, carrying the oldest surviving diagram from Euclid's Elements. The nine lines of Greek state Proposition 5 of Book II: if a straight line is cut into equal and unequal parts, the rectangle contained by the unequal parts, together with the square on the line between the points of section, equals the square on the half. The little figure at the lower right is the rectangle and squares that prove it; in modern notation it is the identity ab + ((a+b)/2 - b)² = ((a+b)/2)². Euclid compiled the Elements in Alexandria around 300 BCE, and it was copied for two thousand years as the model of what a proof should be. This page was written some four centuries after his death, perhaps for a student, and about eight centuries before the oldest complete manuscript of the Elements, which was made in 888.
facts: Written on one side only, in sloping capitals with a few spelling slips, probably from a roll or a loose sheet.
The Elements ran to thirteen books and was printed in more editions than any book but the Bible.
Grenfell and Hunt's Oxyrhynchus finds amount to about half a million papyrus fragments, most still unpublished.
The fragment came to Philadelphia in 1901 as thanks for the university's support of the Egypt Exploration Fund.
